standard.title: The Australian Home Front
standard.description: the effects of the Second World War, with a particular emphasis on the continuities and changes on the Australian home front, such as the changing roles of women and First Nations Australians, and the use of wartime government controls
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have examined the effects of WW1 on the Australian home front including conscription debates, women's roles, and the treatment of returned soldiers (AC9HH9K11). They can apply continuity-and-change analysis. From AC9HH10K01 they understand the political context of Australia's entry into WW2 and the National Security Act 1939. They have not yet examined the specific home front changes of WW2, the distinct position of First Nations Australians in WW2, or the nature of wartime government controls.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students explain the continuities and changes on the Australian home front during WW2, including the changing roles of women and First Nations Australians, and evaluate the effects of wartime government controls on individual rights and freedoms.

nodes.label: Wartime government controls and the suspension of rights
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the major wartime government controls introduced under the National Security Act 1939 and explain their effects on individual rights and freedoms.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two types of wartime government control and explain the effect of each on individual rights.
nodes.typical_width: Students examine the National Security Act 1939 as the legislative basis for wartime controls; describe the range of controls — censorship of media, detention of Japanese, German, and Italian residents, banning of groups opposed to the war, manpower controls; explain the tension between national security and civil liberties; connect conscription through the Citizen Military Forces to the WW1 conscription debates, identifying this as a change from the WW1 approach.
wider: Examine the internment of Japanese, German, and Italian Australians as a case study in the suspension of civil liberties during wartime — analysing the racial and political logic of detention and comparing it with treatment of enemy aliens in other Allied countries
Investigate the Cowra breakout (1944) as a case study in internment conditions and consequences — examining what it reveals about the experience of Japanese POWs and interned civilians in Australia
nodes.hinge_reason: The National Security Act is the structural context for understanding how wartime conditions constrained civilian life — including the specific controls that shaped women's workforce participation (manpower controls) and the treatment of groups targeted by detention orders. Students who lack this structural context cannot evaluate whether home front changes were driven by wartime necessity or pre-existing attitudes, which is the key analytical question in N2–N4.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly accept wartime controls as obviously necessary without examining the tension with civil liberties. Scaffolding this tension — what rights were suspended? who was most affected? were measures proportionate to the threat? — sets up the continuity-and-change analysis in N2–N4.

success_criteria: Describes at least two types of wartime government control and explains the effect of each on individual rights
Explains the introduction of conscription through the Citizen Military Forces as a change from WW1 policy — not merely notes it occurred
Identifies at least one group whose civil liberties were most severely affected by wartime controls

nodes.label: Women's wartime roles — what changed
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe the specific changes to women's roles during WW2 across military and civilian contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Students describe at least two specific changes to women's roles during WW2 — covering at least one military and one civilian example.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate women's roles in the military services (WAAAF, AWAS, WRANS) and in civilian war work — the Women's Land Army, factory work, and voluntary organisations; describe the scale and nature of women's participation; explain what specific barriers were lifted during the war (e.g. employment restrictions, exclusion from particular workplaces) and what formal and informal constraints remained; establish the factual record of change before evaluating its extent in N3.
wider: Investigate the experiences of women in specific service roles — nurses at Singapore, WAAAF radar operators, Women's Land Army workers — examining how day-to-day experience varied across roles and locations
Examine the wartime roles of First Nations Australian women in civilian employment — connecting to N4's content and examining the intersection of gender and racial exclusion in wartime opportunity

response_modes.reason: Students need an accurate factual picture of what changed before they can evaluate the extent of change in N3. Building a repertoire of specific examples across military service, civilian war work, and voluntary roles prevents overgeneralisation in either direction.

success_criteria: Describes at least two specific changes to women's roles during WW2 — covering at least one military and one civilian example
Identifies at least one barrier that was lifted during the war and one that remained

nodes.label: Women's wartime roles — change versus continuity
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the extent to which women's wartime roles represented genuine lasting change versus temporary wartime disruption, using continuity-and-change analysis.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least one change that persisted after the war and at least one that was reversed, and explain the difference in terms of structural versus wartime factors.
nodes.typical_width: Students compare women's roles during the war (N2) with their roles before and after; evaluate which changes persisted and which were reversed when men returned; connect to WW1 precedents (Y9 prior knowledge) to assess whether WW2 represented an acceleration or a repetition of earlier patterns; analyse the structural forces that reversed wartime gains — government policy, social pressure, economic structures; connect forward to K12's women's movement content as the longer-term response to this pattern.
wider: Compare the extent of role change for Australian women with women in Britain or the USA — examining whether the scale and durability of change differed across countries and why
Examine the post-war return to domesticity as a deliberate policy outcome — analysing how government incentives, social messaging, and industrial restructuring combined to reverse wartime gains
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The change-versus-continuity analysis here is a rich application of one of history's core concepts — students must weigh evidence of genuine change against evidence of structural continuity, which is analytically demanding. The connection forward to K12 (women's movement) gives this node genuine longitudinal significance.

response_modes.reason: Students commonly describe wartime changes as straightforwardly progressive — the war liberated women. The continuity dimension (most gains reversed post-war) requires explicit scaffolding. The framework is: what changed during the war? which changes persisted? which were reversed? what does the pattern tell us about the structural limits of wartime change?

success_criteria: Identifies at least one wartime change to women's roles that persisted after the war and at least one that was reversed
Explains the difference in terms of structural versus temporary wartime factors — not merely describes the outcomes
Connects the WW2 pattern to the WW1 precedent — assessing whether WW2 represented acceleration or repetition

nodes.label: First Nations Australians — barriers, inclusion, and service
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can explain the barriers First Nations Australians faced in enlisting, the reasons the government changed its position, and the range of roles First Nations Australians played during the war.
nodes.minimum_width: Students identify at least two barriers to First Nations Australian enlistment; explain at least one reason the government changed its position; describe at least two distinct roles — military and civilian.
nodes.typical_width: Students investigate initial barriers to enlistment (distrust of loyalty, denial of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander status, fears of disharmony); examine the reasons for the government's change in position (critical shortage of soldiers, strategic value of First Nations knowledge and skills in specific environments); investigate the Torres Strait Light Infantry Battalion, the Nackeroos, and the Northern Territory Special Reconnaissance Unit; examine the range of civilian roles — domestic work, ammunition handling, timber cutting, cattle work; evaluate whether wartime inclusion represented genuine recognition of rights or pragmatic necessity.
wider: Examine the contradiction between First Nations Australians serving and dying for a country that denied them citizenship rights — connecting to K09's content on pre-1965 rights campaigns and analysing how wartime service contributed to the post-war rights movement

Investigate the experiences of Torres Strait Islanders specifically — examining how their geographic position gave them a distinct wartime role and how service shaped post-war identity and rights claims
nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The contradiction between service and denied citizenship is one of the most analytically rich threads in the WW2 unit — it connects directly to K09–K11 on First Nations rights campaigns and provides concrete historical evidence for arguments about the relationship between military service and citizenship recognition.

response_modes.reason: The range of roles — military service, specialised units, civilian labour — gives students a more accurate picture than focusing only on combat service. Examining multiple contexts prevents overgeneralisation and builds the evidential base for evaluating the significance of First Nations wartime contribution.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two barriers to First Nations Australian enlistment and explains the reasoning behind each
Explains at least one reason the Australian Government changed its position on First Nations enlistment
Describes at least two distinct roles — military and civilian — that First Nations Australians played, with specific examples

nodes.label: Home front — integrating change, continuity, and significance
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can evaluate the overall effects of WW2 on the Australian home front, integrating the changes to government controls, women's roles, and First Nations participation into a coherent account of what changed, what endured, and what the war's home front significance was.
nodes.minimum_width: Students construct a claim about the home front significance of WW2 that covers at least two of the three areas (government controls, women's roles, First Nations Australians) and explains the relationship between them.
nodes.typical_width: Students draw together N1–N4 to evaluate the overall home front effects: which changes were structural and lasting, which were temporary; how wartime necessity drove changes that prior social structures had prevented; evaluate the extent to which the home front experience of WW2 prepared the ground for the post-war social changes addressed in K07–K13; compare with the WW1 home front to assess whether WW2 represented a greater degree of societal disruption.
wider: Evaluate the home front experience of WW2 from the perspective of different groups simultaneously — arguing whose experience of the home front changed most profoundly and whose was most continuous with pre-war life

Assess the home front legacy of WW2 as a precondition for the post-war rights movements examined in K09–K12 — constructing an argument about the causal relationship between wartime disruption and post-war activism

response_modes.reason: This node draws together the structural context (N1), women's factual changes (N2), change-versus-continuity evaluation (N3), and First Nations experience (N4) into a holistic account. Analytical tasks requiring students to argue across all three areas work well here.

success_criteria: Constructs a claim about the home front significance of WW2 that integrates at least two of the three areas covered in N1–N4
Distinguishes changes that were structural and lasting from those that were temporary — with evidence
Evaluates the home front experience of WW2 in comparison with the WW1 home front, identifying at least one similarity and one difference
